title: The willing are led
hookLine: Cleanthes: the fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling (Letters 107)

lines: DID YOU THINK YOU WERE PROMISED OTHERWISE?
cards: Lucilius has had a bad week. Some of his slaves have run off, and he's written to Seneca full of outrage. Seneca, as usual, doesn't pat him on the head.
Did you think you'd been promised a life without this? You're in a public bath; in a crowd you get jostled and splashed.
Then, at the end of the letter, he sets aside his own words and translates a poem from Greek into Latin verse, five lines by an old Stoic named Cleanthes. The last line is the one to keep.

teach.h: CLEANTHES: A BOXER WHO HAULED WATER.
teach.b: First, the poet. Cleanthes led the Stoic school after its founder, Zeno. The old biographies say he'd been a boxer, and that he hauled water at night to pay for his lessons by day.
His prayer begins, in Seneca's Latin: lead me, father, wherever you wish, and I'll follow without delay. Second, the line.
Seneca ends with this: ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt. The fates lead the willing, and drag the unwilling. It doesn't promise the willing a different road.
The road is the same. The difference is whether you walk it or get pulled along with your heels dug in. Third, a picture later writers used.

teach.h: THE DOG TIED TO THE CART.
teach.b: A dog is tied to a moving cart. It can trot alongside, or it can be hauled. Either way, it goes where the cart goes.
The image is credited to the early Stoics, through a much later Christian writer, so hold its exact source loosely. Fourth, what willing is not.

teach.h: WILLING ISN'T PRETENDING TO LIKE IT.
teach.b: It isn't pretending you like the hard thing, or giving up on changing what can change. Lucilius can still look for his runaways. What he can't do is make the world promise that nobody ever leaves.
Willingness is about the part that has already happened. This week, looking back: what is it for. One body.
On campaign. Gentler than Seneca. For Paulina.

how: Some readers of the Stoics memorize Cleanthes' prayer, in Epictetus' or Seneca's version, and say it before facing something they can't avoid.

o: a Roman general Seneca served under as a youth
an old Stoic, once a boxer, who wrote a prayer
the founder of the Stoic school in Athens

being willing means pretending you like the hard thing
it means not fighting what has already happened.

games.q: you're Lucilius. your slaves have run off and you're furious. what does Seneca send back?
o: a promise that it won't happen again.
a scolding, then a poem: the willing are led.
games.why: he tells him no one was promised otherwise, then ends with Cleanthes: the fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling.

practice: Picture one hard task waiting for you, the postponed call, the form, the conversation, first with your heels dug in: the sighing, the delay, the story about how unfair it is.
Then picture the same task, same difficulty, as you walk toward it, shoulders down, jaw loose, no longer pulling against the rope. If you pray, you can borrow Cleanthes' first words: lead me.

wordCard.voice: Cleanthes. The old Stoic poet whose line Seneca translates: the fates lead the one who's willing, and drag the one who isn't. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca's version of Cleanthes in Letter 107: 'the fates lead the willing'.

carryVoice: Your line: led, not dragged. The road is the same; only the walking changes. See you tomorrow.
